Can a squatter become the owner of a Louisiana house?

Yes, but only after a long stretch of open possession. Louisiana calls it acquisitive prescription, and it takes ten years with good faith and just title, or thirty years without them.

Civil Code article 3473 allows ownership of immovables by ten years of prescription, and article 3475 lists the requisites: ten years of possession, good faith, just title, and a thing that can be acquired this way. Article 3486 allows thirty years of possession without just title or good faith. Someone who simply moves into an empty house usually has neither title nor good faith, so thirty years is the path for a true squatter.

RouteTimeNeedsArticle
Ten year prescription10 yearsGood faith and just titleC.C. 3473, 3475
Thirty year prescription30 yearsPossession onlyC.C. 3486

Article 3488 applies the ten year rules to thirty year prescription where they fit.

What kind of possession counts

Possession has to be physical, visible and unbroken. Under article 3476 the possessor needs corporeal possession, or civil possession that was preceded by corporeal possession.

  • Continuous and uninterrupted.
  • Peaceable, so taking a house by force does not count.
  • Public and unequivocal, so hiding in a vacant house does not count either.

Article 3481 presumes good faith, and a mistake about facts or law does not defeat it. The presumption falls only if the possessor knew or should have known he was not the owner. Under article 3482, good faith matters at the start, and bad faith that develops later does not stop the ten year clock.

These attributes must hold for the entire period, which is why a gap in possession matters.

Just title and why it matters

Just title is a written transfer that would have moved ownership if the seller had really owned the property. It separates a ten year claim from a thirty year one.

Louisiana's transfer without warranty connects here. Article 2502 makes such a transfer a just title for prescription, with no presumption of bad faith. A person who buys rights from someone who did not actually own the house, then possesses it openly, can start the ten year clock. A squatter with no paper at all is stuck on the thirty year route.

If someone has lived on your land for many years, perhaps an unrecorded family member or a neighbor, get a lawyer's view before assuming your title is safe.

Removing an occupant who has no right to be there

The owner gives written notice to vacate and then goes to court by summary rule to show cause. Code of Civil Procedure article 4702 requires written notice once the purpose of the occupancy has ended, and gives the occupant five days from delivery to leave.

Article 4731 covers what comes next. If the occupant does not comply, the owner or agent may summarily cite the occupant to show cause why possession should not be delivered, and the citation must state the grounds. After the required notice, an owner who reasonably believes the premises are abandoned may take possession without more judicial process. The article lists signs such as stopped use, returned keys and removed belongings.

  • After a federal disaster declaration, stopping residential use is not treated as abandonment for 30 days.
  • A residential tenant locked out in violation of the article may recover the greater of $500 or twice the monthly rent.
  • The court may award costs and attorney fees to the winner.

Do not change locks or remove belongings without legal advice. Self help can cost the owner money.

The blighted property rule

R.S. 9:5633.1 lets a possessor acquire blighted property by three years of prescription, but only in certain municipalities, and in Lake Charles with city council approval. It is not a statewide rule.

The property must have been declared blighted after an administrative hearing, and the possessor must file an affidavit and the city's resolution in the mortgage and conveyance records. The owner and every mortgage holder receive certified mail within thirty days, and a notice goes on the building within a month.

  • The possessor must take peaceable possession and begin repairs within a reasonable time, not more than 45 days.
  • All ad valorem taxes, interest and penalties must be paid.
  • Owners of adjoining land have a first right to claim the property.
  • Recorded mortgages and liens are not wiped out.
  • The owner can bring a real action, and must then reimburse the possessor's costs and improvements.

An owner of a neglected house in Lake Charles or another covered city should deal with code citations before they turn into this kind of claim.

Vacant and storm damaged houses

Houses left empty after a storm are the ones most often occupied without permission, and Louisiana has had plenty of storms. The eviction statute reflects this: under article 4731, in parishes covered by a federal disaster declaration, stopping residential use of a home is not treated as evidence of abandonment for 30 days after the declaration.

If you own a damaged house you cannot repair, keep records showing you still hold it, and consider a quick sale before an occupancy problem develops.

A cash sale skips the repair and financing hurdles that damaged houses run into, though the buyer will still want the occupancy question settled before closing. Put the sequence in order: confirm who holds the keys, serve the five day notice if someone is inside without a right to be there, and file the rule to show cause if they stay. Each step leaves a paper trail that a title company will ask to see.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Louisiana houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Before selling a house someone else occupies

Find out who is there and on what basis, then clear the occupancy or disclose it before listing. Possession that has run for years can affect who owns the house.

Article 531 allocates the burden of proof. A person claiming ownership against someone who has possessed for ten years, or for one year in good faith with just title, must prove he acquired ownership from a previous owner or by prescription. In other cases he need only prove a better title. So the length of the occupant's stay decides who carries the burden.

  • Pull the deed and mortgage records from the parish clerk.
  • Write down when the occupant arrived and whether you ever consented.
  • Serve the written notice to vacate and keep proof of delivery.
  • Keep your own tax bills and receipts as evidence that you treat the house as yours.

If you want to sell a Louisiana house with an occupant or a title question, send us the address and we will tell you what we see.

Frequently asked questions

How long does adverse possession take in Louisiana?

Ten years with good faith and just title, or thirty years without them, under Civil Code articles 3473, 3475 and 3486. The possession must also be continuous, peaceable, public and unequivocal.

Do squatters have rights in Louisiana?

Not by moving in. A squatter usually has no title or good faith, so thirty years of possession would be needed. Until then the owner can remove the occupant through a written notice and a rule to show cause.

How much notice must an owner give a non-tenant occupant?

Five days, in writing, once the purpose of the occupancy has ended, under Code of Civil Procedure article 4702. If the person does not leave, the owner may seek a rule to show cause under article 4731.

Does paying property tax stop a squatter from taking my land?

Tax payment is not an element of the possession rules either way. What counts is possession that is uninterrupted, so an owner who sees someone on the land should act early and get legal advice.

Is there a three year adverse possession rule in Louisiana?

Only in narrow cases. R.S. 9:5633.1 allows it for blighted property in certain municipalities and in Lake Charles, with strict notices, repairs and tax payments. Ordinary property follows the ten and thirty year rules.

Louisiana Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

Where Louisiana landlord and tenant rules live

Most of them sit in the Civil Code's lease articles and in the Code of Civil Procedure, with a short deposit statute in Title 9 of the Revised Statutes.

The basic duties are in Civil Code art. 2682. A lessor must hand over the property, keep it in good working condition for its intended use, and protect the lessee's peaceful possession for the whole lease. Those duties do not vanish because the owner decides to sell.

Eviction procedure is in the Code of Civil Procedure, articles 4701 and 4731 through 4733, and it is enforced in justice of the peace, city, parish and district courts. A house with a tenant is a house with a court-supervised process attached to it.

Does a lease survive a sale?

Yes. Civil Code art. 2711 says the lessor's transfer of the leased thing does not terminate the lease, and it gives the tenant a claim against the lessor for any loss the transfer causes.

What the buyer owes the tenant is a separate matter. Under art. 2712, the buyer is not automatically subrogated to the seller's rights under the lease and is not personally bound by the seller's obligations unless the buyer assumes them. Recording is the other half of the answer.

  • Civil Code art. 3338 treats a written lease of an immovable like other instruments affecting real property: without recordation it has no effect as to third persons.
  • Under R.S. 9:2721(B), anyone who acquires an immovable takes it subject to a recorded lease, including terms about commissions owed to a leasing agent, if the lease was recorded before the document that created the acquirer's rights.
  • An unrecorded lease still binds a new owner who assumed it in the purchase agreement or bought at a foreclosure sale, and a buyer can ratify an unrecorded lease by letting the tenant stay and accepting rent.

For a seller, the purchase agreement should say plainly whether the buyer takes the lease. Silence invites a dispute.

Security deposit when a rental is sold

The deposit goes with the property. Under R.S. 9:3251(B), when the landlord's interest is transferred during the lease, the original landlord passes the deposit to the successor, who becomes responsible for returning it at the end of the lease, and the original landlord is relieved of further liability for it.

The ordinary deposit rules still apply to whoever holds it.

  • The deposit is returned within one month after the lease ends.
  • The landlord may keep amounts reasonably needed to remedy a tenant default or unreasonable wear, and must send an itemized statement of reasons within one month of the end of the tenancy, or within fifteen days after that date.
  • The tenant must give a forwarding address when the lease ends.
  • The return rule is off when a tenant abandons the premises without required notice or before the lease ends.
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Louisiana house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Penalty for keeping a deposit

A landlord who willfully fails to comply owes the wrongfully kept amount plus a penalty of $300 or twice that amount, whichever is greater. That is the rule in R.S. 9:3252.

Failing to pay within thirty days after a written demand for a refund counts as willful. A tenant can sue the lessor or the lessor's successor in interest, in the parish where the lessor lives or the parish where the property sits. Under R.S. 9:3253, costs and attorney's fees are left to the court's discretion for the prevailing party.

A sale is where this can go wrong. If a seller spends the deposit and the buyer inherits the liability, the buyer may end up facing a written demand. Handing over the full deposit with a ledger protects both sides.

Notice to end a lease with no fixed end date

The notice depends on the length of the rental period, and the deadlines are counted in calendar days. Civil Code art. 2728 sets them out.

Termination notice for a lease with no definite term
Lease periodNotice before the period ends
Longer than one month30 days
Month to month10 days
At least a week but under a month5 days
Shorter than a weekAny time before the period expires

A timely notice ends the lease at the end of the period it names. If it names none, the lease ends at the close of the first period for which the notice was early enough. A buyer who wants a vacant house usually has to run this clock or negotiate a move-out date in writing.

The notice to vacate

It is the written notice a landlord must give before filing for eviction, and the tenant gets at least five days from delivery to leave. Code of Civil Procedure art. 4701 applies once the tenant's right to occupy has ended, whether by expiration, the landlord's action, nonpayment or some other cause.

  • For a lease with no definite term, the notice that ends the lease also serves as the notice to vacate.
  • For a lease with a definite term, the notice to vacate may be given no more than 30 days before the term expires.
  • A written waiver of notice inside the lease lets the landlord begin eviction proceedings as soon as occupancy ends.

Legal holidays are not counted, so in parishes where weekend days are legal holidays the effective minimum can reach seven days. Courts have also reversed evictions where the notice did not state the grounds in enough detail for the tenant to prepare a defense.

How an eviction case moves through court

After the notice period, the landlord files a rule to show cause, and a judge decides whether the tenant must give up possession. Article 4731 requires the rule to state the grounds, and under art. 4732 the rule may be heard no earlier than the third day after service.

Justice of the peace and district courts hear residential evictions regardless of the rent amount. City and parish courts hear them only within rent limits: under $150 daily, $500 weekly, $3,000 monthly or $36,000 annually. If the tenant does not appear, the court may enter judgment at once, giving 24 hours to vacate. A warrant for possession, carried out by the sheriff, marshal or constable, follows if the tenant stays.

Self-help has a narrow exception. Article 4731(B) lets a lessor retake the premises without a court process after the required notice, but only on a reasonable belief that the tenant abandoned the home. Signs include returned keys and removed belongings. In parishes under a federal disaster declaration, simply ending residential occupancy is not evidence of abandonment for 30 days after the declaration, and a lessor who violates that protection can owe the tenant the greater of $500 or twice the monthly rent.

Before selling a rented house

  • Pull the signed lease and every addendum, and check whether a copy was recorded with the parish clerk.
  • Prepare a deposit ledger showing the amount held and any approved deductions.
  • Decide whether the sale is subject to the lease or will close with the house vacant, and put that decision in writing.
  • If you need the tenant out, count the notice period under art. 2728 or art. 4701 before you set a closing date.
  • Keep rent receipts and repair requests. Under art. 2682 the landlord must keep the home in good working condition, and unrepaired complaints can slow a negotiated move-out.

Owners with a tenant they cannot remove quickly, a lease nobody can find, or a house in poor repair sometimes choose a cash buyer who takes the property as-is and handles the lease terms in the contract. Weigh that only after you know what the lease and deposit actually require.

If the rental is in foreclosure

Foreclosure adds federal and state notice steps for tenants. The sheriff must serve a written notice of seizure on tenants and occupants, and an owner served with the seizure notice has seven days to notify tenants or faces a $200 penalty.

The federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act generally lets a bona fide tenant stay until the lease ends, and requires at least 90 days of written notice when the new owner plans to live in the unit or the tenancy is month to month. A tenant in that position should read the actual lease closely before agreeing to any move-out deal.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Can a Louisiana landlord evict a tenant just because the house was sold?

No. A sale does not end a lease under Civil Code art. 2711. The buyer has to wait for the lease term to end or have grounds such as nonpayment, then give the notice that art. 4701 and art. 2728 require.

How long does a Louisiana landlord have to return a security deposit?

One month after the lease ends. If part is kept, the landlord must send an itemized statement within that month or within fifteen days after it, and the tenant must provide a forwarding address.

How many days notice does a month-to-month tenant need to give?

Ten calendar days before the end of the month, under Civil Code art. 2728. For leases measured by periods longer than a month, the notice is 30 days.

Do I have to record a lease for it to be valid?

No, but an unrecorded lease has no effect against third persons under Civil Code art. 3338. A buyer who did not agree to take it may not be bound, which is why recording and written assumption matter at closing.

Can I change the locks on a tenant who stopped paying rent?

No. Louisiana requires notice and, if the tenant stays, a court rule for possession. The article 4731 exception is limited to a lessor who reasonably believes the tenant has abandoned the premises.

title: Louisiana Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House
content:
Louisiana Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Louisiana Eviction Notice Rules sale

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Louisiana?

Written notice before an eviction

A Louisiana landlord must deliver a written notice to vacate that gives the tenant at least five days from the date of delivery. It applies once the right to occupy has ended, whether because the lease term expired, the landlord acted to end it, rent went unpaid or for any other reason.

The rule is Code of Civil Procedure art. 4701, in the eviction title of the code. The landlord or an agent can send the notice. Because the five days run from delivery, landlords keep a record of when and how the notice was handed over.

The notice comes first and the court filing second. Art. 4731(A) ties the court step to a tenant or occupant who fails to comply with the notice to vacate, or who waived it in the lease.

Notice periods by type of lease or occupant

The period depends on how the lease is measured and who is living in the house. Two laws work together: art. 4701 sets the notice to vacate, and Civil Code art. 2728 sets when a lease with no definite term must be terminated.

Notice timing by situation
SituationNotice or timing
Tenant, lease ended for any reason (C.C.P. art. 4701)Written notice, at least 5 days from delivery
Lease with a fixed termNotice to vacate may go out no more than 30 days before the term ends
Occupant who is not a tenant (art. 4702)Written notice, 5 days from delivery, after the purpose of the occupancy has ended
Term longer than a month (C.C. art. 2728)Termination notice 30 calendar days before the period ends
Month-to-month leaseTermination notice 10 calendar days before the end of the month
Term of a week up to a month5 calendar days before the period ends
Term shorter than a weekAny time before the period expires

How the two notices fit together

For a lease with no fixed end date, a single notice does both jobs. Article 4701 treats the notice the law requires to terminate such a lease as the notice to vacate.

A landlord ending a month-to-month tenancy therefore gives the ten calendar day notice before month's end that art. 2728 describes, and that same notice counts as the notice to vacate. Under art. 2728, a notice given in time ends the lease at the end of the period it names. If it names none, the lease ends at the close of the first period for which the notice was early enough.

A fixed-term lease works differently. The tenant's right ends on the stated date, and the notice to vacate may be delivered up to thirty days before then, but no sooner.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Louisiana house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Who counts as an occupant?

The code's definitions are wider than most owners expect. Under art. 4704, an occupant includes a sharecropper, a half hand, a day laborer and a former owner. It also covers anyone living in the property by permission or accommodation of the owner, a former owner or another occupant, other than a mineral lessee, the owner of a mineral servitude or a lessee of the owner.

That reaches a relative or friend who was allowed to stay. For them, art. 4702 requires the owner to deliver a written notice to vacate once the purpose of the occupancy has ended, with five days from delivery.

The same article defines 'lease' to include oral leases and subleases, and 'lessor' to include a sublessor, assignee or transferee. Someone who buys a rented house can therefore stand in as the lessor, which matters when a landlord sells with a tenant in place.

Waiving the notice in the lease

A tenant can do it. Article 4701 lets a lessee waive the notice requirement in a written waiver contained in the lease. Where that waiver exists, the landlord may begin eviction proceedings immediately when the right to occupy ends for any reason.

Before relying on a waiver, a landlord or buyer should read the lease for:

  • A written waiver clause that is part of the lease itself, since the statute requires it to be there.
  • The lease term, and whether it renews month to month.
  • Any later written changes signed by both parties.

A seller who inherited a rental often has no copy of the lease. Asking the tenant for theirs, along with proof of rent paid, is usually the first step.

If the tenant left or the house looks abandoned

After the required notice, a Louisiana lessor or owner may take possession without going to court on a reasonable belief that the tenant or occupant has abandoned the premises. Art. 4731(B) lists signs of abandonment: ending business activity or residential occupancy, returning the keys, and removing equipment, furnishings or other movables.

Getting it wrong is expensive. Under art. 4731(C)(2), a lessor who fails to comply gives a residential lessee the right to recover $500 or twice the monthly rent, whichever is greater, from the lessor, owner or the lessor's successor in interest. The tenant may also seek a restraining order or preliminary injunction, and the court may award costs and attorney fees to the prevailing party.

Two further limits apply. In parishes under a federal disaster declaration, empty housing is not evidence of abandonment for thirty days after the initial declaration, and a residential tenant seeking a restraining order does not have to post security during those thirty days. None of this overrides the lessor's rights under Civil Code art. 2693.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Louisiana houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Mistakes that make a notice fail

Most problems come from timing, delivery or using the wrong kind of notice. Check each of these:

  • Written, not spoken: arts. 4701 and 4702 both call for written notice.
  • Enough days: five days from delivery is the floor for a notice to vacate.
  • Too early on a fixed term: delivery more than thirty days before the term ends is outside art. 4701.
  • Wrong period for a periodic lease: month-to-month needs the ten day timing in art. 2728, which is separate from the five day minimum.
  • Retaking the house without court when the tenant has not abandoned it: art. 4731(C)(2) gives a residential tenant a $500 or double-rent remedy.

No standard wording is prescribed for the notice, so a landlord's attorney can draft one that states the grounds clearly.

After the notice period ends

If the tenant stays, the owner files for eviction by summary proceeding. Art. 4731(A) lets the lessor or owner cite the occupant by rule to show cause why possession should not be delivered, and the rule must state the grounds. The court sequence, including hearing timing and appeals, is laid out in our Louisiana eviction process guide.

For a seller, the practical question is whether to finish the eviction before listing. A house with a tenant, a stack of notices and a pending hearing is harder to sell on the open market. An as-is cash buyer may take the property with the tenant in place, though that depends on the deal and the lease terms.

Frequently asked questions

How many days notice does a Louisiana landlord have to give to evict?

At least five days from delivery of a written notice to vacate, under Code of Civil Procedure art. 4701. A month-to-month lease also has the ten day termination timing in Civil Code art. 2728.

Is a verbal eviction notice valid in Louisiana?

No. Article 4701 requires written notice to vacate to be delivered to the lessee, and art. 4702 requires written notice to an occupant who is not a tenant.

How much notice does a month-to-month tenant get in Louisiana?

Ten calendar days before the end of the month, under Civil Code art. 2728. With no fixed term, that termination notice also serves as the notice to vacate.

Can a Louisiana lease say the tenant gives up the right to a notice?

Yes. Art. 4701 allows a written waiver in the lease. The landlord can then file immediately once the tenant's right of occupancy ends.

Can a landlord take back the house without court if the tenant left?

Only after the required notice and only on a reasonable belief of abandonment. If the landlord gets it wrong, a residential tenant may recover $500 or twice the monthly rent, whichever is more.
